chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ismail ibn Marrar, from Yunus, from them (peace be upon him), said:

He was asked about a man who killed his slave. He said: If he was not well-known for killing, he would be struck with severe strikes, and the price of the slave would be taken from him and paid to the treasury of the Muslims; and if he was habitual in killing, he would be killed due to it.

key_terms.بَيْتُ مَالِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ: The public treasury of the Muslims
key_terms.قُتِلَ بِهِ: He would be killed due to it (executed)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference in punishment for a master who kills his slave if he is habitual versus if he is not?
ai.summary: This ruling from al-Kafi distinguishes between non-habitual and habitual killers, reflecting the Shia juristic principle that repeated transgression escalates the penalty from financial compensation (diya) to capital punishment (qatl bihi). It highlights the evolution of slave rights in Islamic law, where the master's status as a known offender justifies direct execution rather than mere retribution or compensation.
